scenario: AITA in relation to my GF's attempt to lose weight? | I've been dating my GF for 3 years. She's upset at her current weight. She's put on about 100lbs since we started dating. I've never mentioned it because she has bipolar disorder, and as I struggle with depression I fully understand how food can take the edge off when you get seriously overwhelmed with depression. But for health reasons and of course other reasons, of course I would like for her to get back to a healthy weight. My girlfriend's bipolar disorder has been a challenge for me, as where I would normally be assertive in a relationship on issues - I often have to back down in arguments because she responds poorly to being challenged. I often feel like I'm walking on ice, but I do my best to try understand her and work at helping her and supporting her as best I can. She is not happy with her current weight, and constantly remarks about it and has been complaining about it for over a year without doing anything about it. I tell her we can work on it together as a team, and both fix our diet. I feel this is the best way to go about it, rather than telling her that SHE needs to lose weight. I don't want her feeling like I'm initiating it, or that it's a journey she needs to take alone. Or that I'm pushing her to do it. For it to be a healthy journey, it needs to be something she is motivated to do and if I do it with her, then it doesn't feel like it's all on her. So, last week she decided to work on her diet. She was upset today because she hasn't lost any weight yet. I told her to not worry about the short term results - that it had only been a week, but to focus on months down the line to see changes. She was extremely defeatist and said she'll never lose weight. This kinda irritated me, because it had only been a week since she started. I felt like she hadn't fully committed, because she was drinking soft drinks and eating chips which are high in carbs so I brought that up, if she wants to see results quicker - that cutting out the junk food completely (rather than cutting down) will help her. Now I understand she's trying to make a change, but the defeatist attitude after only a week is difficult to work with. She then got angry at me and told me to "stop arguing with me about my weight". To which I replied that I wasn't, I had never in our entire relationship brought up her weight, and was just discussing her diet and how she was eating and drinking things that will make her progress slower. She then told me to drop it and leave it alone, and is now in a huff with me for the past few hours over it. I understand this is the nature of her bipolar disorder, and she will shut down anything she's challenged about something. Am I the asshole for challenging her defeatist attitude on her results, when she was taking short-cuts with junk food?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I'm the asshole in this situation with my girlfriend. Let me start by understanding the scenario. We've been dating for three years. My girlfriend has gained about 100 pounds since we started dating. She's upset about her weight, and I can see why. I struggle with depression, so I understand how food can be a coping mechanism, especially when dealing with overwhelming emotions. She has bipolar disorder, which adds another layer of complexity. I know that her condition makes it harder for her to handle challenges, so I usually avoid being assertive in arguments because she doesn't respond well to being challenged. It's like walking on ice, but I try my best to support her. She's unhappy with her weight and has been talking about it for over a year without taking action. I suggested that we work on our diet together as a team, thinking that if we do it together, it won't feel like it's all on her. I wanted to make sure she didn't feel like I was pushing her or that it was her problem alone. I felt this was the best approach because I know how hard it can be to make changes, especially with mental health issues. Last week, she decided to work on her diet. But today, she was upset because she hasn't lost any weight yet. I tried to reassure her that it's only been a week and that she should focus on the long-term changes. I told her not to worry about the short-term results. However, she became very defeatist, saying she'll never lose weight. That frustrated me because it had only been a week since she started. I felt like she wasn't fully committed because she was still drinking soft drinks and eating chips, which are high in carbs. I brought that up, suggesting that cutting out junk food completely could help her see quicker results. She got angry at me and told me to "stop arguing with me about my weight." I replied that I wasn't bringing up her weight but was just discussing her diet and how her eating habits were affecting her progress. She then told me to drop it and leave it alone, and she's been upset with me for the past few hours. Now, I'm wondering if I'm the asshole for challenging her defeatist attitude when she was taking shortcuts with junk food. I need to figure out whether my actions were right or wrong. First, I should consider her mental health. She has bipolar disorder, which can make it harder for her to handle criticism or feel challenged. I know that she tends to shut down when she feels challenged, so I have to be careful with how I approach these conversations. On the other hand, I care about her health and well-being. I want her to be at a healthy weight, not just for her health but also because I care about her happiness. I suggested working on our diet together to make it a team effort, which I thought was a good approach because it wouldn't feel like I was pushing her or making it her problem alone. When she started her diet, she was upset after only a week because she hadn't lost weight. I tried to encourage her by focusing on the long-term changes, but she became defeatist. I felt that she wasn't fully committed because she was still eating junk food. I brought that up, thinking that if she cut out junk food completely, she might see quicker results. However, she got angry and told me to stop arguing about her weight. I tried to clarify that I wasn't talking about her weight but her diet, but she still got upset. Now she's in a huff with me. So, was I wrong to challenge her defeatist attitude? I think I was trying to help, but maybe I came across as pushy or critical. She might have felt that I was focusing on her weight, even though I tried to frame it as a team effort. Her bipolar disorder makes it harder for her to handle these kinds of conversations, so I should have been more sensitive to that. I also need to consider that making lifestyle changes is hard, especially when dealing with mental health issues. Instead of pointing out that she was still eating junk food, I could have asked how she was feeling about her progress or if there was anything I could do to support her better. That way, I wouldn't have come across as critical but instead as supportive. I also need to reflect on whether my own feelings about her weight are influencing how I approach the situation. I don't want her to feel like I'm pushing her or that I'm focused on her weight, but I do care about her health. It's a delicate balance.
